ican: I can recognize that every number has a decimal expansion and describe what that expansion looks like for rational and irrational numbers.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Write each number as a decimal: 5/8, 4/11, and √3 (a calculator shows √3 = 1.7320508…). Then describe each decimal as terminating, repeating, or non-repeating and non-terminating.
old_answer: Answer: 5/8 = 0.625 (terminates); 4/11 = 0.3636… (repeats); √3 = 1.7320508… (never ends, never repeats) 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625 — the division stops, so it terminates. 4 ÷ 11 = 0.363636… — the block 36 repeats forever. √3 = 1.7320508… — the digits never end and no block repeats. Terminating and repeating decimals are rational; √3 is irrational.

ican: I can define rational and irrational numbers and give examples of each.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Define a rational number and an irrational number. Then give two examples of each.
old_answer: Answer: Rational = can be written as a fraction of integers (e.g. ¾, −5); irrational = cannot be a fraction, non-repeating non-terminating decimal (e.g. π, √2) Rational: can be written as a fraction a/b of integers (b ≠ 0); its decimal terminates or repeats. Examples: ¾ = 0.75 and −5 = −5/1. Irrational: cannot be written as a fraction; its decimal is non-repeating and non-terminating. Examples: π = 3.14159… and √2 = 1.41421…

ican: I can classify a number as rational or irrational based on whether its decimal terminates, repeats, or is non-repeating and non-terminating.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Classify each number in the table as rational or irrational using its decimal.     Number  Decimal      A  0.48    B  0.555… (the 5 repeats)    C  0.123456789101112… (counting numbers written in order)    D  −7.25
old_answer: Answer: A rational, B rational, C irrational, D rational A: 0.48 terminates → rational. B: 0.555… repeats → rational. C: the digits keep growing (…9, 10, 11, …) so no block ever repeats and it never ends → irrational. D: −7.25 terminates → rational.

ican: I can identify which subset(s) of the real number system a given number belongs to (natural, whole, integer, rational, or irrational).
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: List every subset of the real number system each number belongs to: 0, −12, √64. Choose from natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational.
old_answer: Answer: 0: whole, integer, rational; −12: integer, rational; √64 = 8: natural, whole, integer, rational 0 is not a counting number, but it is whole → whole, integer, rational. −12 is negative, so not whole → integer, rational. √64 = 8 because 8 × 8 = 64, a counting number → natural, whole, integer, rational. None of them is irrational.

ican: I can convert a repeating decimal into its fractional form to show that it is rational.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Jayla divides two whole numbers and her calculator shows 0.185185185… (the block 185 repeats). Use the 9's rule to write this decimal as a fraction in simplest form. Explain how your answer shows the number is rational.
old_answer: Answer: 0.185185… = 185/999 = 5/27, so it is rational The repeating block is 185 — 3 digits. 3 repeating digits → denominator 999; numerator = 185 → 185/999. Simplify: 185 = 5 × 37 and 999 = 27 × 37, so 185/999 = 5/27. Check: 5 ÷ 27 = 0.185185… ✓ It can be written as a fraction of two integers, so it is rational.

ican: I can determine whether a number is rational or irrational from its decimal expansion and justify my classification.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Marcus says 0.12112111211112… is rational "because it has a pattern." (Each time, one more 1 comes before the next 2.) Is Marcus correct? Justify your answer.
old_answer: Answer: No — it is irrational, because it never ends and no block of digits repeats Rational decimals must terminate or repeat the SAME block forever. Here the runs of 1s keep getting longer (1, 11, 111, 1111, …). So no fixed block repeats, and the decimal never ends. A pattern is not the same as repeating → the number is irrational.

ican: I can sort a set of rational and irrational numbers into the correct subsets of the real number system with written reasoning.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Sort the numbers −√25, 0, 18/3, 4.222…, √11, and −1.5 into the real number system. For each number, name every set it belongs to and give a reason.
old_answer: Answer: 18/3: natural, whole, integer, rational; 0: whole, integer, rational; −√25: integer, rational; 4.222… and −1.5: rational; √11: irrational 18/3 = 6, a counting number → natural, whole, integer, rational. 0 is whole but not natural → whole, integer, rational. −√25 = −5 → integer, rational. 4.222… repeats and −1.5 terminates → rational only (not integers). 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 = 3.3166… never ends or repeats → irrational.

ican: I can build and defend a model or graphic organizer of the real number system that shows how natural, whole, integer, rational, and irrational numbers are related.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Describe a nested diagram (graphic organizer) of the real number system using words. Place one number that belongs ONLY in each region: natural; whole but not natural; integer but not whole; rational but not integer; irrational. Then defend your model: why is every natural number also an integer, and why is the irrational set drawn outside the rational set?
old_answer: Answer: Real numbers ⊃ Rational ⊃ Integers ⊃ Whole ⊃ Natural, with Irrational beside Rational; e.g. 4, 0, −3, ⅔, √2 Model: a big Real Numbers box holding two parts — Rational and Irrational. Inside Rational: Integers ⊃ Whole ⊃ Natural (each circle inside the next). Examples: natural 4; whole only 0; integer only −3; rational only ⅔ (0.666…); irrational √2. Every natural number is also an integer because integers are the whole numbers plus their negatives, and the whole numbers include all counting numbers — so the Natural circle sits inside the Integer circle. Irrational sits outside Rational because a number either can be written as a fraction of integers (rational) or cannot (irrational) — it can never be both. Together, Rational and Irrational make up all the real numbers.

ican: I can explain why a number written in fractional form, such as 3π/4, can still be irrational, and justify my reasoning.
title: Rational and irrational numbers
old_question: Devon says, "2π/5 is rational because it is written as a fraction." Explain why Devon is wrong, and compare 2π/5 to 2/5.
old_answer: Answer: 2π/5 is irrational: π is irrational, and multiplying or dividing an irrational number by a nonzero rational number (here 2 and 5) keeps it irrational. 2/5 = 0.4 is a ratio of two integers, so it is rational Rational means it can be written as a fraction of two INTEGERS. 2/5 has integers on top and bottom, so 2/5 = 0.4 is rational. In 2π/5 the top is 2π, which is irrational (not an integer), so this fraction is NOT a ratio of two integers — and it cannot be rewritten as one. Multiplying or dividing an irrational number by a non-zero integer keeps it irrational: 2π/5 ≈ 1.2566370…, never ending or repeating. So looking like a fraction is not enough — 2π/5 is irrational.

ican: I can identify the base and exponent in a power and explain what an exponent represents.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question: In the power 7⁴, name the base and the exponent. Then write 7⁴ as repeated multiplication and find its value.
old_answer: Answer: Base 7, exponent 4; 7⁴ = 7 × 7 × 7 × 7 = 2,401 The base is the number being multiplied: 7. The exponent tells how many times the base is used as a factor: 4. 7⁴ = 7 × 7 × 7 × 7 7 × 7 = 49, 49 × 7 = 343, 343 × 7 = 2,401

ican: I can apply the product of powers, quotient of powers, and power of a power rules to simplify expressions.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question:
Simplify each expression. Write your answer as a single power.
a) 5³ × 5⁶
b) m⁹ ÷ m⁴
c) (k²)⁵
old_answer: Answer: a) 5⁹ b) m⁵ c) k¹⁰ a) Product Rule — same base, multiplying: ADD the exponents. 3 + 6 = 9 → 5⁹ b) Quotient Rule — same base, dividing: SUBTRACT the exponents. 9 − 4 = 5 → m⁵ c) Power Rule — power to a power: MULTIPLY the exponents. 2 × 5 = 10 → k¹⁰

ican: I can evaluate expressions with a zero exponent and rewrite negative exponents as positive powers.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question:
Evaluate or rewrite each expression.
a) Evaluate 9⁰.
b) Rewrite 4⁻³ with a positive exponent, then find its value.
c) Rewrite x⁻⁵ with a positive exponent.
old_answer: Answer: a) 1 b) 1/4³ = 1/64 c) 1/x⁵ a) Any nonzero number to the zero power is 1, so 9⁰ = 1. b) A negative exponent means flip it: 4⁻³ = 1/4³. 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so 4⁻³ = 1/64. c) x⁻⁵ = 1/x⁵

ican: I can multiply and divide monomials by applying the properties of exponents.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question:
Simplify each expression.
a) (6a⁴b)(2a³b⁵)
b) (20x⁸y⁵) ÷ (5x³y²)
old_answer: Answer: a) 12a⁷b⁶ b) 4x⁵y³ a) Multiply coefficients: 6 × 2 = 12. Add exponents on the same base: a⁴ · a³ = a⁷ and b¹ · b⁵ = b⁶ → 12a⁷b⁶ b) Divide coefficients: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Subtract exponents on the same base: x⁸⁻³ = x⁵ and y⁵⁻² = y³ → 4x⁵y³

ican: I can simplify multi-step expressions that combine several exponent properties.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question: Simplify completely: (3a²b³)² · (2ab)³ ÷ (6a⁵b⁸)
old_answer: Answer: 12a²b (3a²b³)² = 3² · a⁴ · b⁶ = 9a⁴b⁶ (the 3 gets squared too). (2ab)³ = 2³ · a³ · b³ = 8a³b³ Multiply: 9 × 8 = 72, a⁴ · a³ = a⁷, b⁶ · b³ = b⁹ → 72a⁷b⁹ Divide by 6a⁵b⁸: 72 ÷ 6 = 12, a⁷⁻⁵ = a², b⁹⁻⁸ = b¹ → 12a²b

ican: I can simplify products and quotients of monomials that include negative or zero exponents.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question:
Simplify. Write your answer using only positive exponents.
(5x⁻²y³)(3x⁶y⁻⁷) ÷ (15x⁰y⁻²)
old_answer: Answer: x⁴/y² Multiply: 5 × 3 = 15, x⁻²⁺⁶ = x⁴, y³⁺⁽⁻⁷⁾ = y⁻⁴ → 15x⁴y⁻⁴ x⁰ = 1, so the divisor is 15y⁻². Divide: 15 ÷ 15 = 1, y⁻⁴⁻⁽⁻²⁾ = y⁻² → x⁴y⁻² Flip the negative exponent: y⁻² = 1/y², so the answer is x⁴/y²

ican: I can analyze and correct errors in another student's use of the exponent rules.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question: Devon simplified (5³)⁴ · 5² ÷ 5⁻⁵ and left his answer as a power of 5. His work is shown in the table. Find each mistake, explain it, and give the correct answer.     Step  Devon's work      1  (5³)⁴ = 5⁷    2  5⁷ · 5² = 5⁹    3  5⁹ ÷ 5⁻⁵ = 5⁴
old_answer: Answer: Correct answer: 5¹⁹ (errors in Step 1 and Step 3) Step 1 error: a power of a power multiplies the exponents, so (5³)⁴ = 5¹², not 5⁷. Step 2: 5¹² · 5² = 5¹⁴ (same base, add exponents). Step 3 error: dividing subtracts exponents, and 14 − (−5) = 19, not 9 − 5. Correct: 5¹⁴ ÷ 5⁻⁵ = 5¹⁹

ican: I can explain why a⁰ = 1 and why a negative exponent represents a reciprocal, connecting the rules to repeated multiplication.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question:
Use repeated multiplication with base 5 to explain:
a) why 5⁰ = 1, and
b) why 5⁻² = 1/25.
Then explain why a⁰ = 1 works for any base a except 0.
old_answer: Answer: 5³ ÷ 5³ = 1 = 5⁰ and 5² ÷ 5⁴ = 1/5² = 5⁻²; works for any a ≠ 0 a) 5³ ÷ 5³ = (5·5·5) ÷ (5·5·5) = 1, since every factor cancels. The Quotient Rule gives 5³⁻³ = 5⁰. Both are the same expression, so 5⁰ = 1. b) 5² ÷ 5⁴ = (5·5) ÷ (5·5·5·5). Cancel 2 pairs, leaving 1/(5·5) = 1/25. The Quotient Rule gives 5²⁻⁴ = 5⁻². So 5⁻² = 1/5² = 1/25. Pattern check: 5² = 25, 5¹ = 5, 5⁰ = 1, 5⁻¹ = 1/5, 5⁻² = 1/25 — each step down divides by 5. For any base: aⁿ ÷ aⁿ = 1 and also = a⁰, so a⁰ = 1. This needs a ≠ 0 because you cannot divide by 0.

ican: I can construct and evaluate complex expressions using the properties of exponents, justifying each step with mathematical reasoning.
title: Properties of integer exponents
old_question: Rewrite (2⁵ · 4²)³ ÷ 8⁴ as a single power of 2, then find its value. Name the rule or reason for each step.
old_answer: Answer: 2¹⁵ = 32,768 Rewrite with the same base: 4 = 2², so 4² = (2²)² = 2⁴ (Power Rule); 8 = 2³, so 8⁴ = (2³)⁴ = 2¹² (Power Rule). Inside the parentheses: 2⁵ · 2⁴ = 2⁹ (Product Rule: add 5 + 4). (2⁹)³ = 2²⁷ (Power Rule: multiply 9 × 3). 2²⁷ ÷ 2¹² = 2¹⁵ (Quotient Rule: subtract 27 − 12). 2¹⁵ = 2¹⁰ × 2⁵ = 1,024 × 32 = 32,768

ican: I can explain that squaring and square rooting are inverse operations.
title: Square roots and cube roots
old_question: Kai squares a positive number and gets 196. Then he takes the square root of 196. What number does he end with, and what does this show about squaring and square rooting?
old_answer: Answer: He ends with 14; squaring and square rooting are inverse operations — they undo each other The starting number was 14, since 14² = 196. √196 = 14, so he is back to the number he started with. Square rooting undid the squaring: they are inverse operations.

ican: I can classify a square root as rational or irrational based on whether the radicand is a perfect square.
title: Square roots and cube roots
old_question: Classify each square root as rational or irrational: √36, √40, √1, √150, √169.
old_answer: Answer: Rational: √36, √1, √169; irrational: √40, √150 Perfect squares: 36 = 6², 1 = 1², 169 = 13² → √36 = 6, √1 = 1, √169 = 13 (rational). 40 and 150 are not perfect squares (they fall between 36 & 49 and 144 & 169). So √40 and √150 are irrational.

ican: I can represent solutions to equations of the form x² = p and x³ = p.
title: Square roots and cube roots
old_question:
Solve each equation. Leave any irrational answer as a root.
a) x² = 121
b) x³ = −27
c) x² = 30
old_answer: Answer: a) x = ±11 b) x = −3 c) x = ±√30 a) 11² = 121 and (−11)² = 121, so x = 11 or x = −11. b) Take the cube root: x = ∛(−27) = −3, because (−3)(−3)(−3) = −27. Only one answer. c) 30 is not a perfect square, so x = √30 or x = −√30. Check: (√30)² = 30 ✓

ican: I have my perfect squares and cubes (and their inverses) up to 20 memorized.
title: Square roots and cube roots
old_question: Without a calculator, evaluate √289 + ∛343 − √361. Then Lena says ∛216 = 8. Is she right? Explain.

ican: I can construct and evaluate complex expressions involving square roots, cube roots, and integer exponents, justifying each step with mathematical reasoning.
title: Square roots and cube roots
old_question: Evaluate (√169 − ∛125)² ÷ 2³ + √(36 + 64). Justify each step. Then explain why √(36 + 64) is NOT equal to √36 + √64.
old_answer: Answer: 18; √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10, but √36 + √64 = 14 √169 = 13 and ∛125 = 5, so the parentheses give 13 − 5 = 8. 8² = 64 and 2³ = 8, so 64 ÷ 8 = 8. The root acts like a grouping symbol: add first, √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. 8 + 10 = 18. √36 + √64 = 6 + 8 = 14 ≠ 10 — you cannot split a square root over addition.

ican: I can apply square and cube roots to real-world problems involving area and volume, and I have my perfect squares and cubes (and their inverses) up to 40 memorized.
title: Square roots and cube roots
old_question: (a) A square patio has an area of 361 square feet. How long is each side? (b) A cube-shaped box holds 343 cubic inches. How long is each edge, and what is the area of one face? (c) Explain why you used a square root in part (a) and a cube root in part (b).
old_answer: Answer: (a) 19 ft (b) edge 7 in; face area 49 in² (a) Area of a square = side², so side = √361 = 19 ft (19 × 19 = 361). (b) Volume of a cube = edge³, so edge = ∛343 = 7 in (7 × 7 × 7 = 343). One face is a 7-by-7 square: 7² = 49 in². (c) Area uses the side twice (squared), so a square root undoes it. Volume uses the edge three times (cubed), so a cube root undoes it.

ican: I can write a number in scientific notation as a coefficient (≥ 1 and < 10) times a power of 10.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question:
Write each number in scientific notation.
a) 82,000,000
b) 0.00000415
old_answer: Answer: a) 8.2 × 10⁷ b) 4.15 × 10⁻⁶ a) Move the decimal LEFT until it sits after the first nonzero digit: 8.2. That is 7 hops. Large number → positive exponent: 8.2 × 10⁷ b) Move the decimal RIGHT to land after the 4: 4.15. That is 6 hops. Small number (< 1) → negative exponent: 4.15 × 10⁻⁶

ican: I can convert between scientific notation and standard (decimal) notation.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question:
Convert each number.
a) 2.07 × 10⁶ to standard form
b) 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ to standard form
c) 304,000 to scientific notation
old_answer: Answer: a) 2,070,000 b) 0.00063 c) 3.04 × 10⁵ a) Positive exponent: hop the decimal 6 places right, filling with zeros → 2,070,000 b) Negative exponent: hop the decimal 4 places left, filling with zeros → 0.00063 c) Move the decimal 5 places left to get 3.04 → 3.04 × 10⁵

ican: I can use scientific notation to estimate very large and very small quantities.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question: A video website had 3,912,450,000 visits in one month. A dust particle is 0.0000738 meters wide. Estimate each quantity as a single digit times a power of 10.
old_answer: Answer: About 4 × 10⁹ visits; about 7 × 10⁻⁵ m 3,912,450,000 = 3.91245 × 10⁹ (9 hops left). Round the coefficient to one digit: about 4 × 10⁹ visits. 0.0000738 = 7.38 × 10⁻⁵ (5 hops right). Round the coefficient to one digit: about 7 × 10⁻⁵ m.

ican: I can compare two quantities in scientific notation and tell how many times as large one is than the other.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question: A city has about 8 × 10⁶ people. A small town has about 2 × 10⁴ people. How many times as many people live in the city as in the town?
old_answer: Answer: 4 × 10² = 400 times as many Divide the larger by the smaller: (8 × 10⁶) ÷ (2 × 10⁴). Divide coefficients: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Subtract exponents: 6 − 4 = 2 → 4 × 10² 4 × 10² = 400

ican: I can order several quantities written in scientific notation.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question: The table shows the approximate widths of five tiny things. Order them from smallest to largest.     Object  Width (m)      Pollen grain  2.5 × 10⁻⁵    Red blood cell  8 × 10⁻⁶    Human hair  9 × 10⁻⁵    Dust mite  3 × 10⁻⁴    Bacterium  2 × 10⁻⁶
old_answer: Answer: Bacterium, red blood cell, pollen grain, human hair, dust mite Compare exponents first. All are negative; the most negative is smallest: 10⁻⁶ < 10⁻⁵ < 10⁻⁴. 10⁻⁶ group: 2 × 10⁻⁶ < 8 × 10⁻⁶ → bacterium, then red blood cell. 10⁻⁵ group: 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ < 9 × 10⁻⁵ → pollen grain, then human hair. 10⁻⁴: 3 × 10⁻⁴ → dust mite is largest.

ican: I can estimate and compare the magnitude of two quantities and express one as a multiple of the other.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question: A hit song has been streamed 2,987,000,000 times. A new song has been streamed 4,890,000 times. Round each number to a single digit times a power of 10. About how many times as many streams does the hit song have?

ican: I can analyze and correct errors in scientific-notation form (coefficient not between 1 and 10, or the wrong sign on the exponent).
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question: Three students tried to write numbers in scientific notation. Each answer has a mistake. Explain each mistake and write the correct scientific notation.     Student  Number  Student's answer      Jada  0.00071  7.1 × 10⁴    Marcus  386,000  38.6 × 10⁴    Lena  0.00052  0.52 × 10⁻³
old_answer: Answer: Jada: 7.1 × 10⁻⁴; Marcus: 3.86 × 10⁵; Lena: 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ Jada: 0.00071 is less than 1, so the exponent must be negative → 7.1 × 10⁻⁴. Marcus: 38.6 is not less than 10. Move the decimal left one more place and add 1 to the exponent → 3.86 × 10⁵. Lena: 0.52 is less than 1. Move the decimal right one place and subtract 1 from the exponent → 5.2 × 10⁻⁴.

ican: I can choose appropriate units and use scientific notation to make sense of very large or very small real-world measurements, justifying my reasoning.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question:
A sheet of paper is about 0.0001 m thick. The Moon is about 384,000,000 m from Earth.
a) Write each in scientific notation in meters.
b) Rewrite the paper thickness in millimeters and the Moon distance in kilometers (1 m = 1,000 mm; 1 km = 1,000 m).
c) Which unit would you choose to report each measurement? Justify your choice.
old_answer: Answer: Paper: 1 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.1 mm (use mm); Moon: 3.84 × 10⁸ m = 3.84 × 10⁵ km (use km) a) 0.0001 m = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m (4 hops right); 384,000,000 m = 3.84 × 10⁸ m (8 hops left). b) Paper: 1 × 10⁻⁴ × 10³ = 1 × 10⁻¹ mm = 0.1 mm. Moon: 3.84 × 10⁸ ÷ 10³ = 3.84 × 10⁵ km = 384,000 km. c) Choose a unit that is close in size to the thing being measured, so the number is easy to picture: millimeters for paper, kilometers for the Moon. Scientific notation in meters is still useful when comparing both in the same unit; the exponents show the Moon distance is about 10¹² times the paper thickness.

ican: I can explain how the exponent shows the order of magnitude and use it to reason about how many times as large one quantity is than another.
title: Scientific notation to estimate and compare
old_question: An ant has a mass of about 3 × 10⁻⁶ kg. An elephant has a mass of about 6 × 10³ kg. Kai says, "The exponents are 9 apart, so the elephant is about 10⁹ times as heavy as the ant." Explain what the exponents tell you, decide whether Kai's reasoning makes sense, and find the actual number of times as heavy.
old_answer: Answer: Kai's order of magnitude is right; the elephant is 2 × 10⁹ (2 billion) times as heavy The exponent tells the order of magnitude: each increase of 1 means 10 times as large. From 10⁻⁶ to 10³ is 3 − (−6) = 9 steps, so the masses differ by about 10⁹. Kai's estimate makes sense. For the exact multiple, also divide the coefficients: (6 × 10³) ÷ (3 × 10⁻⁶) = (6 ÷ 3) × 10³⁻⁽⁻⁶⁾ = 2 × 10⁹. The coefficients only change the answer by a factor of 2, so 10⁹ is a good estimate; the actual answer is 2 billion times.

ican: I can identify a linear equation, recognize the role of variables, coefficients, and constants, and apply inverse operations to isolate the variable and solve a linear equation in one variable.
title: Equations and inequalities in one variable
old_question: Look at the equation 4x − 7 = 21. Explain why it is a linear equation. Name the variable, the coefficient, and the constant on the left side. Then solve it using inverse operations.
old_answer: Answer: Linear (x has an exponent of 1); variable x, coefficient 4, constant −7; x = 7 It is linear because x is only to the first power (no x², no x in a denominator). Variable: x. Coefficient: 4. Constant: −7. Undo − 7 by adding 7: 4x = 28. Undo × 4 by dividing by 4: x = 7. Check: 4(7) − 7 = 28 − 7 = 21 ✓

old_question: Three students each simplified a different equation until the steps ended. Student A ended with x = 4. Student B ended with 0 = 6. Student C ended with −3 = −3. How many solutions does each student's equation have?

old_question: Solve (3/4)(x − 8) = (1/2)x + 1. Then check your answer by substitution.
old_answer: Answer: x = 28 (both sides equal 15) Distribute 3/4: (3/4)x − 6 = (1/2)x + 1 Subtract (1/2)x: (1/4)x − 6 = 1 Add 6: (1/4)x = 7 Multiply by 4: x = 28 Check: (3/4)(20) = 15 and (1/2)(28) + 1 = 15 ✓

ican: I can recognize when equations have no solution or infinitely many solutions, and mathematically determine whether a linear equation has one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions.
title: Equations and inequalities in one variable
old_question:
Decide whether each equation has one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions. Show your work.
A) 4(x − 3) + 2 = 4x − 10
B) 5x − 2(x + 1) = 3x + 7
C) 6x + 1 = 2(2x − 3) + 3
old_answer: Answer: A: infinitely many; B: no solution; C: one solution (x = −2) A: 4x − 12 + 2 = 4x − 10 → 4x − 10 = 4x − 10 → −10 = −10 TRUE → infinitely many. B: 5x − 2x − 2 = 3x + 7 → 3x − 2 = 3x + 7 → −2 = 7 FALSE → no solution. C: 6x + 1 = 4x − 6 + 3 → 6x + 1 = 4x − 3 → 2x = −4 → x = −2 → one solution. Check C: 6(−2) + 1 = −11 and 2(−7) + 3 = −11 ✓

ican: I can explain and justify the solution type (one, none, or infinite) with mathematical reasoning.
title: Equations and inequalities in one variable
old_question: Ava solved 2(3x − 4) + 5 = 6x − 3. The x's cancelled, so she said, "There is no solution." Is Ava correct? Explain your reasoning. Then change ONE number on the right side so the equation truly has no solution, and explain why it has none.
old_answer: Answer: Ava is wrong: it has infinitely many solutions. Example fix: 2(3x − 4) + 5 = 6x + 1 has no solution. Simplify the left: 6x − 8 + 5 = 6x − 3, so both sides are the exact same expression. Subtract 6x: −3 = −3, a TRUE statement, so every value of x works → infinitely many solutions (e.g., x = 0 gives −3 = −3). Ava's mistake: the x's cancel in BOTH special cases; you must check whether what is left is true or false. Change −3 to +1: 6x − 3 = 6x + 1 → −3 = 1, FALSE. For any x, 6x − 3 is always 4 less than 6x + 1, so the sides can never be equal → no solution.

b) Solve the system and explain what the solution means for her business.

old_answer: Answer: Cost y = 2x + 300, income y = 8x; break-even at (50, 400); $180 profit for 80 shirts Cost: y = 2x + 300 (start $300, plus $2 per shirt). Income: y = 8x (start $0, plus $8 per shirt). Graph both lines or make a table: at x = 50, cost = 2(50) + 300 = 400 and income = 8(50) = 400, so the lines cross at (50, 400). Meaning: at 50 shirts her cost and income are both $400, so she breaks even (no profit, no loss). Fewer than 50 shirts: cost line is higher, so she loses money. a) Write Kim’s equation. Will they ever have the same amount of money? Explain using the graphs of the two lines and using algebra.
b) What would Kim’s starting amount have to be for the system to have infinitely many solutions? Explain what the graph would look like.
old_answer: Answer: a) No — y = 15x + 25 is parallel to Jada’s line, so there is no solution b) $40 — the lines would be the same line Kim: y = 15x + 25. Both lines have slope 15 but different y-intercepts (40 and 25), so the lines are parallel. Parallel lines never cross, so there is no point that is on both lines: no solution. Jada is always $15 ahead. Algebra: 15x + 40 = 15x + 25 → 40 = 25, which is false, so no value of x works. If Kim started with $40, her equation would be y = 15x + 40, the same line as Jada’s. The two lines would lie on top of each other, so every point works in both: infinitely many solutions (they always have the same amount).

old_answer: Answer: −√6 ≈ −2.4, √3 ≈ 1.7, √8 ≈ 2.8, π ≈ 3.1 (order: −√6, √3, √8, π) √6: 4 < 6 < 9, between 2 and 3; calculator 2.449… → 2.4, so −√6 ≈ −2.4 (left of 0, just right of −2.5). √3: 1 < 3 < 4, between 1 and 2; 1.732… → 1.7. √8: 4 < 8 < 9, between 2 and 3, close to 3; 2.828… → 2.8. π = 3.14159… → 3.1, just to the right of 3. ican: I can explain and model an estimation algorithm for square roots of non-perfect squares and defend the accuracy of my approximation.
title: Approximating irrational numbers
old_question: Use the estimation algorithm to estimate √33 to the nearest tenth. Explain why each step works, then defend the accuracy of your answer by squaring.
old_answer: Answer: √33 ≈ 5.7 Trap it: 25 < 33 < 36, so √33 is between 5 and 6 — the root must sit between the roots of the surrounding perfect squares. Fraction: (33 − 25) ÷ (36 − 25) = 8 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.73 — 33 is 8 of the 11 steps from 25 to 36, so √33 is about that far from 5 to 6. Add: 5 + 0.73 = 5.73 → about 5.7. Defend: 5.7² = 32.49 and 5.8² = 33.64, so √33 is between 5.7 and 5.8. The midpoint 5.75² = 33.0625 > 33, so √33 < 5.75 and rounds to 5.7. Calculator check: √33 = 5.744… → 5.7 ✓

b) How many liters does each home get in a 30-day month?

old_question:
Each hair on a person's head grows about 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ m per day. A person has about 1 × 10⁵ hairs.

b) How many days would it take for the combined growth to reach 7 × 10³ m?

old_answer: Answer: a) 3.5 × 10¹ m per day (35 m) b) 2 × 10² days (200 days) a) Every hair grows the same amount, so multiply growth per hair by the number of hairs: (3.5 × 10⁻⁴)(1 × 10⁵). 3.5 × 1 = 3.5 and −4 + 5 = 1 → 3.5 × 10¹ m per day = 35 m per day. Units: (m per hair per day) × hairs = m per day. b) To find how many days fit into the total, divide total length by length per day: (7 × 10³) ÷ (3.5 × 10¹). 7 ÷ 3.5 = 2 and 3 − 1 = 2 → 2 × 10² days. Units: m ÷ (m per day) = days. Check: 35 m per day × 200 days = 7,000 m = 7 × 10³ m ✓

When multiplying powers of 10 you ADD them. b) (2.5 × 10³)(1 × 10³) = 2.5 × 10³⁺³ = 2.5 × 10⁶ kg c) (2.5 × 10⁶) ÷ (1 × 10³) = 2.5 × 10³ metric tons = 2,500 t. old_answer: Answer: A: linear; B: nonlinear; C: linear A: y goes up 3 each time x goes up 1 — a constant change, so linear. B: x is squared, so it is nonlinear (y-values 1, 2, 5, 10 do not change by the same amount). C: the graph is a straight line, so it is linear.

old_answer: Answer: A: positive; B: zero; C: undefined; D: negative A: y goes up as x goes up (uphill) → positive. B: y stays 5 (horizontal) → zero. C: x stays 6 (vertical) → undefined. D: y goes down as x goes up (downhill) → negative.

ican: I can recognize y = mx + b as the slope-intercept form of a linear equation, identifying m as slope and b as y-intercept.
title: Identify linear functions
old_question: Each equation is in slope-intercept form, y = mx + b. Name m (slope) and b (y-intercept) for each: (a) y = 5x − 3  (b) y = −x + 8  (c) y = ¾x
old_answer: Answer: (a) m = 5, b = −3 (b) m = −1, b = 8 (c) m = ¾, b = 0 m is the number in front of x; b is the number added on. (a) y = 5x + (−3), so b = −3. (b) −x means −1x, so m = −1. (c) Nothing is added, so b = 0.

ican: I can find the slope and y-intercept from an equation, a graph (determining slope using rise over run), or a table.
title: Identify linear functions
old_question: A line on a graph passes through (0, −3) and (2, 5). Use rise over run to find the slope. Then give the y-intercept.
old_answer: Answer: Slope = 4; y-intercept = −3 Start at (0, −3) and move to (2, 5). Rise: up from −3 to 5 = 8. Run: right from 0 to 2 = 2. Slope = rise/run = 8/2 = 4. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, −3), so b = −3.

old_answer: Answer: (a) steeper (b) shifts down 5 (c) goes downhill, same steepness (a) m changes from 2 to 5, so the line is steeper. It still crosses at (0, 1). (b) b changes from 1 to −4, so the line moves down 5. Same slope, so it is parallel. (c) m changes from 2 to −2, so the line now falls left to right with the same steepness. Still crosses at (0, 1).

old_answer: Answer: A → Graph 2, B → Graph 1, C → Graph 3; in A, $25 per month and a $50 sign-up fee. A has b = 50 and m = 25 → Graph 2. B has b = 0 and m = 50 → Graph 1. C: 25(2) = 50, so (2, 50) is on it → Graph 3. In A, slope 25 = cost per month ($25); y-intercept 50 = one-time fee at 0 months ($50).

ican: I can explain how the structure of y = mx + b represents a linear function with a constant rate of change.
title: Identify linear functions
old_question: Explain why y = 4x + 3 has a constant rate of change. Show that when x goes up by 1, y always goes up by 4, no matter what x you start at. Then explain why y = x² is different.
old_answer: Answer: y always increases by 4 for each +1 in x, so the rate is constant and the graph is a straight line. At any x, y = 4x + 3. At x + 1, y = 4(x + 1) + 3 = 4x + 7. The difference is (4x + 7) − (4x + 3) = 4, for every x. The b-value 3 is added to every y, so it never changes the differences; only m sets the rate. For y = x²: 0, 1, 4, 9 change by 1, 3, 5 — not constant, so it is not linear.

ican: I can use algebraic or graphical reasoning to develop slope-intercept form from an incomplete representation (e.g., a table missing the y-intercept).
title: Identify linear functions
old_question: This linear table is missing the row for x = 0, and the x-values do not go up evenly. Find the slope and the y-intercept, and write the equation in slope-intercept form. Explain how you know b.     x  y      3  7    5  10    9  16
old_answer: Answer: y = 1.5x + 2.5 From (3, 7) to (5, 10): m = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5. From (5, 10) to (9, 16): 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 ✓ (constant rate). Work back from (3, 7) to x = 0: x drops 3, so y drops 3(1.5) = 4.5. b = 7 − 4.5 = 2.5 (same as b = y − m·x). Equation: y = 1.5x + 2.5. Check x = 9: 13.5 + 2.5 = 16 ✓

ican: I can identify the rate of change (slope) and initial value (y-intercept) from linear functions given as graphs, tables, equations, or verbal descriptions.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question: The table shows the height of a sunflower, in centimeters, x weeks after it was planted in the garden. Find the rate of change (slope) and the initial value (y-intercept).     Weeks (x)  Height in cm (y)      0  12    1  17    2  22    3  27
old_answer: Answer: Slope = 5 cm per week; y-intercept = 12 cm Each time x goes up 1, y goes up 5 (12 → 17 → 22 → 27). So the slope m = 5 ÷ 1 = 5. When x = 0, y = 12, so b = 12. Equation: y = 5x + 12.

ican: I can explain that slope represents rate of change and y-intercept represents initial value, and recognize that the y-intercept can represent a starting value in real-world applications.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question: A taxi ride costs y = 2.50x + 4 dollars, where x is the number of miles. What does 2.50 mean? What does 4 mean? Which one is the starting value?
old_answer: Answer: 2.50 = $2.50 per mile (rate of change); 4 = $4 starting fee (initial value) 2.50 is the slope: the cost goes up $2.50 for each mile. 4 is the y-intercept: the cost when x = 0 miles. So $4 is the starting fee you pay before the taxi moves.

ican: I can compare the rate of change and initial values of two linear functions presented in different formats, using input/output pairs to make basic comparisons.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question: Two pools are being filled. Pool A’s water depth in inches is d = 2h + 7, where h is hours. Pool B’s depth is shown in the table. Which pool fills at a faster rate? Which pool started with more water?     Hours (h)  Depth in inches (d)      0  1    1  4    2  7    3  10
old_answer: Answer: Pool B fills faster (3 in/hr > 2 in/hr); Pool A started with more water (7 in > 1 in) Pool A: m = 2, b = 7. Pool B: each hour the depth goes up 3 (1 → 4 → 7 → 10), so m = 3. Pool B: at h = 0, d = 1, so b = 1. Compare: 3 > 2, so B is faster; 7 > 1, so A started deeper.

ican: I can identify and compare slope and y-intercept in graphs, tables, mappings, and equations of linear models.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question:
Three linear functions are shown in different ways.
Function A (graph): a straight line that passes through (0, −3) and (2, 5).
Function B (mapping): 1 → 6, 2 → 9, 3 → 12, 4 → 15.
Function C (equation): y = −2x + 10.
List the functions from greatest slope to least slope. Which function has the greatest y-intercept?
old_answer: Answer: Slopes: A (4), B (3), C (−2); C has the greatest y-intercept (10) A: slope = (5 − (−3)) ÷ (2 − 0) = 8 ÷ 2 = 4; y-intercept = −3. B: each input up 1, output up 3, so slope = 3; b = 6 − 3(1) = 3. C: slope = −2, y-intercept = 10. Order of slopes: 4 > 3 > −2. Greatest y-intercept: 10 > 3 > −3, so C.

ican: I can use information from linear models to identify trends and associations between input/output pairs and make general predictions.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question: Jordan watches videos on a tablet. The table shows the battery level as he watches. The pattern is linear. Is the association positive or negative? Predict the battery level after 100 minutes, and predict when the battery will reach 0%.     Minutes watched (x)  Battery % (y)      0  90    20  80    40  70    60  60
old_answer: Answer: Negative; 40% after 100 minutes; 0% after 180 minutes Battery drops 10% every 20 minutes, so slope = −10 ÷ 20 = −0.5 (% per minute). As minutes go up, battery goes down: a negative association. Model: y = −0.5x + 90. x = 100: y = −0.5(100) + 90 = 40%. y = 0: 0 = −0.5x + 90 → 0.5x = 90 → x = 180 minutes.

ican: I can use algebra to find missing values required to compare functions.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question:
Function A is linear and is shown in the table, but one input is missing. Function B is y = 4x − 3.
a) Write the equation for Function A and find the missing input k.
b) Which function has the greater initial value? Which has the greater rate of change?
c) Use algebra to find the input where both functions have the same output. Explain how you know.     x  y      2  7    5  16    k  25
old_answer: Answer: A: y = 3x + 1, k = 8; A has greater initial value, B has greater rate; equal at (4, 13) Slope of A: (16 − 7) ÷ (5 − 2) = 9 ÷ 3 = 3. b = 7 − 3(2) = 1, so y = 3x + 1. Missing input: 25 = 3k + 1 → 24 = 3k → k = 8. Initial values: A is 1, B is −3, so A starts higher. Rates: B is 4, A is 3, so B grows faster. Set equal: 3x + 1 = 4x − 3 → 4 = x. Output: 3(4) + 1 = 13 and 4(4) − 3 = 13. Before x = 4, A is greater; after x = 4, B is greater because its slope is bigger.

ican: I can use comparisons of linear models to make predictions using mathematical language and supporting evidence.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question: Mia and Jon run a 200-meter race. Mia gets a 30-meter head start and runs 5 meters per second, so her distance is d = 5t + 30. Jon starts at the starting line; his distances are in the table. Predict who wins. Support your answer with the rates, the time each runner finishes (round to the nearest tenth of a second), and when (if ever) one runner passes the other.     Time in seconds (t)  Jon’s distance in meters (d)      0  0    2  14    4  28    6  42
old_answer: Answer: Jon wins: he passes Mia at 15 s (105 m) and finishes in about 28.6 s vs Mia’s 34 s Jon’s rate: 14 m every 2 s = 7 m/s, so d = 7t. Mia’s rate is 5 m/s with a 30 m head start. Jon catches up because his rate is greater: 7t = 5t + 30 → 2t = 30 → t = 15 s, at d = 105 m. Mia finishes: 5t + 30 = 200 → t = 34 s. Jon finishes: 7t = 200 → t ≈ 28.6 s. Mia’s head start only helps at first; after 15 s Jon is always ahead, so Jon wins.

ican: I can identify the significance of specific input/output pairs and explain how they are relevant in context.
title: Compare two linear functions
old_question: Ava gets a $240 gift card for a video game store. She spends $15 every week. Her balance is y = −15x + 240 after x weeks. Explain what each of these points means in this situation: (0, 240), (10, 90), and (16, 0). Then explain why the point (20, −60) does not make sense here.
old_answer: Answer: (0, 240) start balance; (10, 90) $90 left after 10 weeks; (16, 0) card empty at week 16; (20, −60) is impossible (0, 240): at week 0, before spending, the card has $240 (the initial value / y-intercept). (10, 90): after 10 weeks she has spent $150, so $90 is left. Check: −15(10) + 240 = 90. (16, 0): after 16 weeks the card is empty (x-intercept). Check: −15(16) + 240 = 0. (20, −60): a gift card cannot have a negative balance, so the model only makes sense from x = 0 to x = 16.

ican: I can recognize when a real-world or mathematical situation can be modeled with a linear function.

old_question: Which situations can be modeled with a linear function? A: A pool has 100 gallons and fills at 20 gallons per minute. B: A number of bacteria doubles every hour. C: A taxi charges $3 plus $2 per mile. D: The area of a square with side length s.
old_answer: Answer: A and C are linear; B and D are not. A: adds 20 gallons every minute — constant rate → linear. B: doubling adds more each hour — not constant → nonlinear. C: adds $2 every mile — constant rate → linear. D: A = s² — squared → nonlinear.

ican: I can use the slope formula to calculate slope from two coordinate points.
title: Model linear relationships
old_question: Use the slope formula to find the slope of the line through (−3, 8) and (5, −4). Kayla got 3/2 by writing (−4 − 8) ÷ (−3 − 5). What was her mistake?
old_answer: Answer: m = −3/2; Kayla subtracted the x-values in the opposite order from the y-values. m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁). m = (−4 − 8) ÷ (5 − (−3)) = −12 ÷ 8 = −3/2. Kayla used y₂ − y₁ on top but x₁ − x₂ on the bottom. Both must subtract in the same order, so her sign is wrong.

old_answer: Answer: y = −0.03x + 12.1; 4.6 gallons left after 250 miles m = (8.5 − 11.2) ÷ (120 − 30) = −2.7 ÷ 90 = −0.03 gallon per mile. b = 11.2 − (−0.03)(30) = 11.2 + 0.9 = 12.1 gallons. Slope: the car uses 0.03 gallon each mile. y-intercept: the tank started with 12.1 gallons. Check (120, 8.5): −3.6 + 12.1 = 8.5 ✓ At 250 miles: −0.03(250) + 12.1 = −7.5 + 12.1 = 4.6 gallons.

Week  Plan A ($)  Plan B ($)      0  20  1    1  30  2    2  40  4    3  50  8    4  60  16    5  70  32
old_answer: Answer: Plan A is linear (+$10 each week); Plan B is not (doubles). Plan B passes Plan A in week 7. Plan A adds $10 every week — a constant rate, so it is linear: y = 10x + 20. ican: I can read a graph to identify where a function is increasing, decreasing, or constant.

old_answer: Answer: Increasing 0–10 s; constant 10–25 s and 40–50 s; decreasing 25–40 s Rising (going up left to right) means increasing: 0 to 10 s. Flat means constant: 10 to 25 s and 40 to 50 s. Falling means decreasing: 25 to 40 s.

Part 2: a horizontal straight segment from (2, 6) to (5, 6).
Part 3: a curve from (5, 6) to (8, 15) that bends and gets steeper.
Classify each part as linear or non-linear.
old_answer: Answer: Part 1 linear; Part 2 linear; Part 3 non-linear A straight line (any direction, even flat) is linear. Part 1 is straight → linear. Part 2 is straight and flat → linear. Part 3 curves → non-linear.

ican: I can describe intervals of increase, decrease, and constancy using correct interval language.
title: Qualitative graphs
old_question: A graph shows a hiker’s elevation (feet) over time (hours). It is made of straight pieces: from (0, 500) up to (2, 1,500), flat to (3, 1,500), up to (5, 2,300), then down to (8, 500). Use interval language to describe where the graph is increasing, decreasing, and constant. Which increasing interval is steeper?
old_answer: Answer: Increasing from x = 0 to x = 2 and from x = 3 to x = 5; constant from x = 2 to x = 3; decreasing from x = 5 to x = 8. The piece from x = 0 to x = 2 is steeper. Increasing (going up left to right): from x = 0 to x = 2 and from x = 3 to x = 5. Constant (flat): from x = 2 to x = 3. Decreasing (going down): from x = 5 to x = 8. Rates: (1,500 − 500) ÷ 2 = 500 ft per hour; (2,300 − 1,500) ÷ 2 = 400 ft per hour. 500 > 400, so the first piece is steeper.

ican: I can explain whether a section of a graph is linear or non-linear by referring to its rate of change.

old_question: The table gives points from a graph of a hot-air balloon’s height over time. Is the section from 0 to 3 minutes linear or non-linear? Is the section from 3 to 6 minutes linear or non-linear? Explain using the rate of change.     Time (min)  Height (m)      0  0    1  20    2  40    3  60    4  70    5  90    6  120
old_answer: Answer: 0–3 min is linear (constant rate 20 m/min); 3–6 min is non-linear (rate changes) 0 to 3 min: height goes up 20, 20, 20 each minute. The rate is constant, so it is linear. 3 to 6 min: height goes up 10, then 20, then 30 each minute. The rate keeps changing, so this section is non-linear (it curves and gets steeper).

old_answer: Answer: Rises from 0 for 30 s, flat for 2 min, falls more steeply to 0 over 20 s, then flat at 0 for 40 s Axes: Time (s) on x, Speed on y. Start at speed 0. 0–30 s: graph rises (speeding up). 30–150 s: horizontal line (constant speed). 150–170 s: graph falls to 0, steeper than the rise because it slows in less time. 170–210 s: flat along speed 0 (waiting at the station).

ican: I can analyze a graph and explain what its features mean in the context of the real-world situation.
title: Qualitative graphs
old_question:
A graph shows the gallons of gas in a car’s tank over time (hours).
• From 0 to 2 hours it falls steadily from 14 to 8 gallons.
• From 2 to 2.5 hours it is flat at 8 gallons.
• From 2.5 to 3 hours it rises steeply from 8 to 14 gallons.
• From 3 to 5 hours it falls steadily from 14 to 10 gallons.
Explain what each part means in this situation. Why is the last part less steep than the first part?
old_answer: Answer: Driving, stopped, filling up at a gas station, then driving while using gas more slowly (2 gal/hr vs 3 gal/hr) Start: the tank has 14 gallons at time 0 (the y-intercept). 0–2 h: the car is driving and using gas at (14 − 8) ÷ 2 = 3 gallons per hour. 2–2.5 h: gas stays at 8, so the car is parked and not using gas. 2.5–3 h: gas goes up fast, so the driver is filling the tank back to 14. 3–5 h: driving again at (14 − 10) ÷ 2 = 2 gallons per hour. The last part is less steep because gas is used more slowly (for example, slower driving), so the rate of change is smaller.

ican: I can sketch and justify a non-linear graph and explain why the rate of change is not constant.

Explain why the graph is non-linear, using the rate of change.     Time (s)  Height (m)      0  100    1  95    2  80    3  55    4  20
old_answer: Answer: A curve starting at (0, 100) that falls slowly at first then faster and faster; non-linear because the drop per second grows Sketch: start at (0, 100); the curve goes down, gentle at first, then steeper, ending near (4, 20). Drops each second: 100 → 95 is 5 m, 95 → 80 is 15 m, 80 → 55 is 25 m, 55 → 20 is 35 m. The rate of change is not the same each second (5, 15, 25, 35), so the graph is not a straight line. In context: the ball speeds up as it falls, so it loses more height each second and the curve gets steeper.

ican: I can use complementary, supplementary, vertical, and adjacent angle relationships to find missing angles.
title: Angle relationships
old_question:
Lines AB and CD cross at point E. ∠AEC = 58°.
a) Find ∠BED, ∠AED, and ∠CEB.
b) Separately, ∠P and ∠Q are complementary and ∠P = 34°. Find ∠Q.
old_answer: Answer: ∠BED = 58°, ∠AED = 122°, ∠CEB = 122°, ∠Q = 56° ∠BED is vertical to ∠AEC, so ∠BED = 58°. ∠AED and ∠AEC are adjacent and form a linear pair: 180° − 58° = 122°. ∠CEB is vertical to ∠AED, so ∠CEB = 122°. Complementary angles add to 90°: ∠Q = 90° − 34° = 56°.

ican: I can identify the angle pairs formed when parallel lines are cut by a transversal (corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior, same-side interior) and state whether they are congruent or supplementary.
title: Angle relationships
old_question:
Lines j and k are parallel (j ∥ k) and are cut by transversal t. Line j is above line k. The table shows where the eight angles are. For each pair, name the angle pair type and say whether the angles are congruent or supplementary.
a) ∠2 and ∠6
b) ∠4 and ∠5
c) ∠1 and ∠8

By the theorem, that right triangle's hypotenuse squared is a² + b² = c², so its hypotenuse is c. The two triangles have the same three side lengths, so they match exactly (one fits right on top of the other). So the first triangle also has a right angle, across from side c.

Rotate 90° clockwise, (x, y) → (y, −x): T(1, 1), U(1, 3), V(4, 1). Translate (x + 2, y − 6): T(3, −5), U(3, −3), V(6, −5) — these are K, L, M ✓ Each step is a rigid transformation, so side lengths and angles never change (check: TU = KL = 2, TV = KM = 3). Since a sequence of rigid transformations maps △TUV exactly onto △KLM, the triangles are congruent. (Other correct sequences are possible.)

Rotate 90° counterclockwise, (x, y) → (−y, x): A(−3, 3), B(−3, 9), C(−6, 3) = D, E, F ✓ A sequence of a dilation and a rigid move maps △ABC onto △DEF, so △ABC ~ △DEF. The rotation changes nothing about size or angles; the dilation keeps every angle and multiplies every side by 3. So ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F, and DE/AB = DF/AC = 3 (6/2 = 3/1 = 3).

ican: I can explain why dilations produce similar (not congruent) figures and how the scale factor affects side lengths and area.
title: Transformations with coordinates
old_question:
Rectangle WXYZ has W(0, 0), X(4, 0), Y(4, 3), Z(0, 3). It is dilated by a scale factor of 3 about the origin.
a) Give the image coordinates.
b) Compare the side lengths, perimeter, and area of the two rectangles.
c) Explain why a dilation makes a similar figure but not a congruent one, and why the area grows by more than 3 times.
old_answer: Answer: W′(0, 0), X′(12, 0), Y′(12, 9), Z′(0, 9); sides and perimeter ×3 (14 → 42); area ×9 (12 → 108) (x, y) → (3x, 3y) gives W′(0, 0), X′(12, 0), Y′(12, 9), Z′(0, 9). Sides 4 and 3 become 12 and 9 (×3). Perimeter 14 → 42 (×3). Area 4 × 3 = 12 → 12 × 9 = 108, which is 9 = 3² times as big. A dilation keeps every angle (still 90°) and multiplies every side by the same k, so the shape is the same but the size is not → similar, not congruent. Area uses two lengths (length × width), and each is multiplied by k, so area is multiplied by k · k = k².

Decide whether each association would most likely be linear or non-linear. Justify your thinking.
A) The number of movie tickets bought (at $12 each) and the total cost.

old_answer: Answer: A is linear; B is non-linear. A: Each extra ticket always adds $12, a constant rate of change, so the points fall on a straight line. old_question: The height of a young oak tree is modeled by y = 0.5x + 3, where x is the age in years and y is the height in feet. Predict the tree's height at 12 years. About how old will it be when it is 13 feet tall?
old_answer: Answer: About 9 feet at 12 years; about 20 years old at 13 feet. Substitute x = 12: y = 0.5(12) + 3 = 6 + 3 = 9 feet. Set y = 13: 0.5x + 3 = 13. Subtract 3: 0.5x = 10. Divide by 0.5: x = 20 years.

old_question: A gym charges a $25 sign-up fee plus $30 per month. Write a linear model for the total cost y after x months. Use it to find the cost for 8 months and how many months it takes for the total to reach $295. Describe the trend.
old_answer: Answer: y = 30x + 25; $265 for 8 months; 9 months to reach $295; the cost rises $30 each month. The rate of change is $30 per month (slope); the starting value is $25 (y-intercept). Model: y = 30x + 25. 8 months: y = 30(8) + 25 = 240 + 25 = $265. $295: 30x + 25 = 295 → 30x = 270 → x = 9 months. Trend: positive and linear; the total grows by $30 every month.

old_question: A candle's height is modeled by y = −1.5x + 24, where x is hours burning and y is height in centimeters. Identify the slope and y-intercept and tell what each means. Then find the height after 6 hours and how long until the candle burns out.
old_answer: Answer: Slope −1.5 (loses 1.5 cm per hour); y-intercept 24 (starts 24 cm tall); 15 cm after 6 hours; burns out after 16 hours. Slope = −1.5: the candle gets 1.5 cm shorter each hour. y-intercept = 24: the candle is 24 cm tall before it is lit. 6 hours: y = −1.5(6) + 24 = −9 + 24 = 15 cm. Burned out means y = 0: −1.5x + 24 = 0 → 1.5x = 24 → x = 16 hours.

old_question: The table shows a child's height each year. (a) Write a linear model using a line of best fit through (2, 34) and (10, 54). (b) Use it to predict the height at age 12 and at age 30. (c) Evaluate whether each prediction is reasonable.     Age (years)  Height (in.)      2  34    3  36    4  39    5  42    6  44    7  46    8  50    9  52    10  54
old_answer: Answer: y = 2.5x + 29; age 12 ≈ 59 in. (reasonable); age 30 ≈ 104 in. (not reasonable). Slope = (54 − 34) ÷ (10 − 2) = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5; then 34 = 2.5(2) + b, so b = 29. Model: y = 2.5x + 29. Age 12: 2.5(12) + 29 = 59 in. (about 4 ft 11 in.), close to the data, so it is reasonable. Age 30: 2.5(30) + 29 = 104 in. (8 ft 8 in.), which is not realistic. The model only works for the ages in the data; people stop growing in their late teens, so the trend does not continue. Predictions far beyond the data range (extrapolation) can be unreliable.
